chapter_summary:
Welcome to the exciting world of animation in Blender! This chapter introduces you to the core concept of keyframe animation, which is the foundation for bringing your static 3D models to life. At its heart, keyframe animation involves defining specific states of an object (its position, rotation, or scale) at particular points in time. Blender then intelligently calculates the in-between frames, creating smooth motion. Think of it like a flipbook: you draw the first page and the last page, and Blender draws all the pages in between.

To begin animating, you'll primarily interact with the **Timeline editor** at the bottom of the Blender interface. This horizontal strip represents the duration of your animation, marked by frames. A typical animation might run at 24 or 30 frames per second (fps), a setting you can adjust in the Output Properties panel. The red vertical line, known as the playhead, indicates the current frame. You can drag the playhead to scrub through your animation, or use the playback controls (play, pause, next/previous frame) located at the bottom of the Timeline.

The process of setting a keyframe is straightforward. First, select the object you wish to animate. Then, move the playhead to the desired starting frame (e.g., frame 1). Position, rotate, or scale your object as needed for its initial state. With the object selected, press the `I` key (for 'Insert Keyframe') in the 3D Viewport. A menu will appear, asking you what properties you want to keyframe. For basic movement, you'll often choose 'Location', 'Rotation', 'Scale', or 'LocRotScale' to keyframe all three simultaneously. Once a keyframe is set, a yellow diamond will appear on the Timeline at the current frame, indicating that the object's properties are "keyed" at that point.

Now, advance the playhead to a later frame (e.g., frame 50). Move, rotate, or scale your object to its new desired state. Press `I` again and insert another keyframe for the same properties. When you drag the playhead back and forth, you'll observe Blender interpolating the movement between these two keyframes, creating a smooth transition. This is the essence of keyframe animation: defining critical poses, and letting the software fill in the gaps. You can continue this process, adding more keyframes at different points in time to create complex movements.

Blender offers various **interpolation types** which dictate how the software calculates the motion between keyframes. By default, Blender uses 'Bezier' interpolation, which creates smooth, organic curves, often resulting in natural-looking acceleration and deceleration. If you select a keyframe on the Timeline (or in the Dope Sheet, which we'll discuss shortly) and press `T`, you'll see options like 'Linear', 'Constant', 'Bezier', 'Cubic', and more. 'Linear' interpolation creates a constant speed between keyframes, resulting in very mechanical motion. 'Constant' interpolation holds the value of a keyframe until the next keyframe is reached, creating sudden, jerky changes, useful for things like blinking lights or sudden object appearances. Understanding and choosing the right interpolation type is crucial for conveying the desired feeling of your animation.

A powerful feature to speed up your workflow is **Auto Keying**. Located in the Timeline editor, it's represented by a red circle icon. When enabled, any transformation (location, rotation, scale) you apply to an object while the playhead is not on an existing keyframe will automatically insert a new keyframe for those properties. If you modify an object on an existing keyframe, it will update that keyframe. This can be incredibly convenient for quickly blocking out animation, but it also carries a common mistake: accidentally keyframing unwanted changes. Always be mindful of the auto-keying state and the current frame when making adjustments to your scene. It's a good practice to toggle it off once you've set your initial key poses and are moving into refinement, or to use it judiciously for specific tasks.

Beyond the Timeline, the **Dope Sheet editor** provides a more detailed view of your keyframes. You can switch to the Dope Sheet from the editor type selector (top-left of any editor window). The Dope Sheet shows all keyframes for all animated objects, organized by object and then by property (e.g., Cube > Location X, Location Y, Location Z). This editor allows you to select, move, scale, and delete multiple keyframes simultaneously, making it easier to adjust timing and rhythm across your entire animation. For instance, you can select a group of keyframes, press `G` to move them in time, or `S` to scale their timing, effectively speeding up or slowing down a section of animation. This level of control is essential for polishing your animated sequences.

Common mistakes beginners make include forgetting to set keyframes, leading to objects snapping back to their original positions; accidentally overwriting keyframes by not moving the playhead; or using only 'Linear' interpolation, which makes animations look robotic. Always double-check your keyframes and use the Dope Sheet to get a clear overview of your animation data. Remember, animation is an iterative process. Don't be afraid to experiment, play back your animation frequently, and refine your keyframes until the motion feels just right.

screens.title: Introduction to Keyframe Animation
screens.subtitle: Bring static models to life by defining poses in time and letting Blender interpolate motion.

narration.text: Welcome — in this session you'll learn the core idea behind keyframe animation and why it underpins almost every motion you create in Blender. Keyframe animation means recording an object's properties, like position, rotation, or scale, at specific frames. Blender then calculates the frames between those key moments so the object moves smoothly. This is the same principle that powers flipbooks, but with precise control over timing and interpolation. You will also learn how to use the Timeline to place and scrubb keyframes, switch to the Dope Sheet to edit many keys at once, choose interpolation types to change motion quality, and use Auto Keying to speed up blocking phases. As a concrete example, you will build a simple bouncing ball: set a high pose on frame 1, low on frame 20, and watch Blender interpolate the arc. A common beginner mistake is relying only on linear motion, which looks mechanical; learning interpolation types like Bezier gives life to movement. By the end of this chapter you will be able to set keyframes, adjust timing, and avoid accidental keying, giving you the foundation to animate characters, props, and cameras with confidence.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Keyframes record important poses at specific frames; Blender interpolates the in-between frames to create motion.

Explore Key Topics

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Core Skills
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives focus on the practical skills you will build while learning keyframe animation. First, you will understand the fundamental principles of keyframes: defining poses at frames and relying on interpolation to generate motion. Knowing this concept helps you plan timing and spacing before you key anything. Second, you will navigate the Timeline and Dope Sheet editors — the Timeline is for playback and basic key placement while the Dope Sheet is for selecting and adjusting many keys at once. Third, you will set, move, and delete keyframes for an object's location, rotation, and scale using the insert-key command and editor tools. Practically, this means you can block a pose on frame 1 and a new pose on frame 20 and watch Blender interpolate. Fourth, you will differentiate interpolation types like Linear, Constant, and Bezier so you can control the feel of motion. For example, swapping Linear for Bezier adds ease-in and ease-out, making motion feel more natural. Each skill ties to an immediate practice: try the bouncing ball and then open the Dope Sheet to edit timing. Which objective do you want to try first?

screens.subtitle: How to apply these objectives in your Blender session

narration.text: Now let's connect those objectives to a simple workflow you can practice immediately. Start by planning three or four key poses for any motion — these are the frames you'll key. Use the Timeline to position the playhead on the desired frame and insert a keyframe for Location, Rotation, or Scale. If you want to record several transforms at once, choose LocRotScale. After you have a few keys, open the Dope Sheet to see all keys across objects, select groups, press G to move them in time, or S to scale timing. To explore motion quality, select a key and press T to try Linear, Bezier, or Constant interpolation and watch how motion speed changes. Use Auto Keying only when quickly blocking poses; otherwise disable it to avoid accidental keys. Practice: create a bouncing ball, then open the Dope Sheet and shift the contact frames earlier or later — notice how rhythm changes. This hands-on approach connects the objective cards to real steps and helps you internalize when to key, when to adjust, and when to polish.

screens.title: What is a Keyframe?
screens.subtitle: Definition, analogy, and why key poses matter

narration.text: A keyframe is a recorded snapshot of an object's property values at a specific frame. It marks the exact values for location, rotation, or scale at that moment. Think of keyframes as punctuation marks in a sentence: they indicate the important moments that give motion its structure. When you set a keyframe for a cube's location at frame 1 and a different location at frame 50, Blender interpolates the intermediate positions so the cube travels smoothly. A concrete example: key the Z-position of a sphere on frame 1 at a height of 2 units, then key frame 20 at Z = 0 to create a landing. A common misconception is that every frame must be keyed; you only need the essential poses. Over-keying creates clutter and makes global timing harder to adjust. Another mistake is forgetting to be on the intended frame when inserting a key, causing values to be recorded in the wrong place. Keyframes matter because they let you separate posing from timing: first decide the poses that communicate weight and intention, then time them using the Timeline and Dope Sheet. Ask yourself: which two or three poses most clearly define the action you want to show?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A keyframe records property values at a frame; use only the poses essential to convey the motion's intent.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › What is a Keyframe?
Core Concept

Keyframe — a snapshot in time

A marker that stores an object's property values at a specific frame so Blender can interpolate between keys.

Analogy: Keyframes are punctuation marks for motion — use them to define the important beats.
Concrete example
Set Z-location key at frame 1 (Z=2), set another at frame 20 (Z=0). Playback reveals the fall created by interpolation.
Key Takeaway

Keyframes are minimal: pick only what you need to describe motion concisely.

Common mistake

Over-keying every frame makes later timing edits tedious and unpredictable.

Visualized steps
Select object Move playhead to frame 1 Transform object (e.g., move Z to 2) Press I → choose 'Location' to insert keyframe Move playhead to frame 20 Move object to Z=0 Press I → choose 'Location'
Use this small recipe to create your first two key poses and observe how Blender fills frames between them.
Try this
Set only the high and low poses for a bounce, then adjust timing before adding more keys.

screens.title: Using the Timeline Editor
screens.subtitle: Playback, scrub, and place keyframes for timing control

narration.text: The Timeline editor is your primary interface for controlling playback and placing keyframes along a sequence. It represents time horizontally with numbered frames and shows keyframes as diamond markers. The playhead indicates the current frame and can be dragged to scrub through the animation or stepped frame-by-frame. A small but essential practice is to decide the frames where key poses belong before inserting keys. For example, when blocking a bouncing ball, set the playhead to frame 1 for the initial high pose and press the insert key command to record location. Then move the playhead to frame 20 for contact and set another key. The Timeline also shows playback controls to preview motion at project frames per second. A common misconception is that insertion always creates new keys even when you intend to update an existing key; in fact, if the playhead is already on an existing keyframe, inserting will replace that key's values. Use the Timeline's auto-key toggle carefully: when enabled, any transform you make on a frame without a key will create one. This speeds up blocking but can clutter your animation if left on during refinement. Ask yourself: have I set the playhead precisely where I want the change to be recorded?

keyIdea.title: Timeline purpose
keyIdea.text: Control playback, scrub frames, and place or update keyframes — it's where you shape overall timing.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Using the Timeline Editor
Process Flow

Timeline workflow

Use the Timeline to position the playhead, insert or update keys, and play back your scene to evaluate timing.

Step 1 — Scrub and plan
Drag the playhead to the frame where a key pose should sit. Accurate placement prevents accidental overwrites.
Step 2 — Insert or update
Press the insert-key action and select which properties to record, or rely on Auto Keying when blocking.
Tip
If you're updating a pose, ensure the playhead is exactly on the keyframe to replace the values instead of creating a duplicate.
Visual guide
Timeline concept strip: [Frame 1] ◊ yellow diamond (key) [Frame 20] ◊ yellow diamond (key) Playhead → vertical red line indicates current frame
Example scenario
Set initial pose at frame 1, contact at frame 20, tweak spacing by dragging the keys along the timeline to change rhythm.
Key Takeaway

The Timeline is where you decide when motions happen; accurate playhead placement prevents accidental keys.

Common mistake

Leaving Auto Keying on during detailed edits creates many unwanted keyframes.

screens.title: Inserting and Managing Keyframes
screens.subtitle: How to set, update, and delete Location, Rotation, and Scale keys

narration.text: Inserting keyframes is the action that captures an object's current transform at a chosen frame. The common workflow is: select the object, move the playhead, transform the object to the desired pose, then insert a keyframe for the chosen properties. In Blender, the insert-key command opens a menu where you can choose Location, Rotation, Scale, or LocRotScale to record multiple properties at once. If you insert on a frame that already has a key for that property, Blender updates the existing key instead of creating a second marker. To delete a key, select the key in the Timeline or Dope Sheet and remove it; this reverts the animation to the surrounding keys. A practical example: to animate a door, you might key rotation on frame 1 at 0 degrees and again on frame 20 at 90 degrees. Deleting an intermediate or accidental key restores the interpolation between the remaining keys. Beware of overwriting: many beginners move an object on the wrong frame and insert a key, unintentionally changing an earlier pose. Familiarize yourself with selection and deletion in the Dope Sheet for safe bulk edits and recoverability. Which transform do you want to practice inserting first?

keyIdea.title: Key management
keyIdea.text: Insert keys with intent for Location, Rotation, Scale; update on-frame keys and delete unwanted keys in editors.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Inserting and Managing Keyframes
Definition

Insert, update, and delete keys

Capture transforms at frames. Update keys by inserting on the same frame, delete keys to remove unwanted poses.

Example sequence: Select object Move playhead to frame 1 Transform object to pose A Press 'I' → choose 'Location' to insert Move to frame 20 Transform to pose B Press 'I' → choose 'Location' Select key → Delete to remove unwanted pose
Supporting notes
  • Use LocRotScale to record all three transforms when you need a full-pose snapshot.
  • If you want to change a key's value, be sure the playhead is on the keyframe so insertion updates the key.
  • Deleting a key restores the interpolation between the remaining keys; this can be useful for simplification.
Key Takeaway

Insert keys deliberately and update on-frame keys to avoid accidental duplicates.

Common mistake

Moving the object off-frame then inserting creates a key at the wrong time; confirm the playhead first.

screens.title: Interpolation Types
screens.subtitle: How Linear, Constant, and Bezier change motion quality

narration.text: Interpolation determines how Blender calculates the frames between two keyframes. The three often used types are Linear, Constant, and Bezier. Linear interpolation moves a value at a constant rate between keys — it gives a mechanical, unvarying speed. For example, sliding a cube from X=0 to X=5 with Linear will look like a steady slide. Constant interpolation holds the previous value until the next key is reached, then snaps; this is useful for instant changes such as blinking lights or abrupt property switches. Bezier interpolation creates smooth curves with ease-in and ease-out behavior, producing natural acceleration and deceleration that often reads as lifelike motion; a bouncing ball benefits from Bezier because it simulates gravity and inertia. A common misconception is to stick with Linear because it's predictable; while predictable, Linear often looks artificial. To practice, set a simple horizontal motion with the same two keys and toggle between Linear and Bezier to hear the difference in feel. The takeaway: choose interpolation to match the physical or stylistic intent of the motion, then refine control points if finer timing is needed.

keyIdea.title: Interpolation matters
keyIdea.text: Choose the interpolation type to control speed and feel between keyframes: Linear, Constant, or Bezier.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Interpolation Types
Comparison

Linear vs Constant vs Bezier

Linear
Constant speed between keys. Use for mechanical, even motion.
Constant
Hold until the next key, then snap. Useful for instant changes or discrete states.
Bezier
Smooth ease-in/ease-out curves for organic motion. Preferred for lifelike animation.
Practical example
Create two keys for X position and test each interpolation. Linear = steady slide. Bezier = slide with easing. Constant = step change.
Misconception
Assuming one interpolation fits all motions. Instead, match interpolation to the physical or stylistic intent of the action.
Key Takeaway

Interpolation shapes speed. Swap types to test different emotional or physical readings of motion.

Pro tip

Use Bezier for natural motion and linear for mechanical motion. Tune Bezier handles for precise easing.

screens.title: Auto Keying: Speed vs Risk
screens.subtitle: When to use Auto Keying and how to avoid accidental keys

narration.text: Auto Keying is a workflow convenience that automatically inserts or updates keyframes when you change an object's transform while the playhead is on a frame without an existing key. It lets you quickly block poses without manually inserting keys each time. For example, during the early blocking stage of a walk cycle you might enable Auto Keying and make large pose changes at successive frames to capture major beats quickly. The convenience comes with risk: every minor tweak you make while Auto Keying is active can create unwanted keyframes, cluttering the Timeline and making later adjustments harder. A common mistake is leaving Auto Keying on when refining a pose: small accidental nudges will be recorded as additional keys. To avoid this, toggle Auto Keying off during fine edits and use manual insertion for deliberate keys. Another safe practice is to monitor which channels Auto Keying will affect — some editors allow channel filtering. Practically, use Auto Keying to block, then switch it off to polish. Reflect: did Auto Keying speed your blocking, or did it introduce noisy keys you later had to delete?

keyIdea.title: Auto Keying
keyIdea.text: Auto Keying records transforms automatically while enabled; use it for fast blocking but turn it off to avoid accidental keys.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Auto Keying: Speed vs Risk
Definition

Auto Keying explained

When enabled, transforms you make on frames without keys automatically create new keyframes for the active channels.

Use case: Quickly block poses for a walk cycle by moving through frames and adjusting limbs with Auto Keying on.
Risk
Small unintended adjustments will be recorded, creating noisy curves and extra keys to clean up later.
Practical guardrails
  • Enable Auto Keying for rough blocking, then disable when refining.
  • Check the playhead before large edits to avoid creating keys at the wrong frame.
  • Use Dope Sheet to quickly delete accidental keys created by Auto Keying.
Key Takeaway

Auto Keying speeds blocking but requires discipline; toggle it off for cleaning and refinement.

Pro tip

Use Auto Keying with channel filters or only during dedicated blocking passes to reduce noise.

screens.title: Dope Sheet Essentials
screens.subtitle: Organize, select, move, and scale groups of keyframes

narration.text: The Dope Sheet gives you a bird's-eye view of all keyframes in your scene, organized by object and property. It is the primary editor for adjusting timing across multiple keys or objects at once. You can select a range of keys and press G to move them earlier or later in time, or press S to scale their spacing and thus speed up or slow down a section. For example, select all Z-location keys of a bouncing ball and scale their spacing to compress the bounce into fewer frames, creating a quicker rhythm. The Dope Sheet also allows you to select many keys across different objects and delete or duplicate them, which is essential when polishing complex scenes. Beginners often assume keys are independent per object; in the Dope Sheet you can see how keys from different objects line up and affect the overall rhythm. Another common error is moving keys without visual playback checks; always scrub or play back after bulk edits to ensure you didn't break the motion. The Dope Sheet lets you refine timing more globally than the Timeline, making it a powerful tool for rhythm and choreography.

keyIdea.title: Dope Sheet use
keyIdea.text: Use the Dope Sheet to edit many keyframes at once: move, scale, delete, and align keys for global timing control.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Dope Sheet Essentials
Architecture

Dope Sheet overview

A timeline view that lists keyframes per object and property, enabling batch edits to timing and rhythm.

Select and move
Select a group of keys and press G to reposition them in time across the scene.
Scale timing
Press S to compress or expand keys' spacing, effectively changing speed for the selection.
Concrete example
Select all Z-location keys for the ball, press S and type 0.8 to tighten timing for a faster bounce sequence.
Misconception
Assuming a single edit affects only one object; Dope Sheet edits can impact multiple objects simultaneously if selected.
Key Takeaway

Use the Dope Sheet for global timing edits like moving or scaling groups of keys to change rhythm quickly.

Pro tip

After bulk edits, scrub or play back immediately to catch any unintended timing shifts.

screens.title: Bouncing Ball: Step-by-Step
screens.subtitle: A guided activity to apply keyframes, interpolation, and the Dope Sheet

narration.text: Let's apply these concepts with the bouncing ball exercise. Start a new Blender file, delete the default cube, and add a UV Sphere named BouncingBall. Move the playhead to frame 1, lift the ball on the Z-axis to a high pose, and insert a Location key. Next, move the playhead to frame 20, bring the ball down to touch the ground at Z = 0 and insert a Location key. Repeat at frame 40 with a slightly lower height, frame 60 at ground, and frame 80 with an even smaller bounce. Play the animation to observe the basic blocking. Now open the Dope Sheet, select all Z-location keys, and press T to experiment with Linear and Bezier interpolation: Linear will create a mechanical bounce, Bezier will give you a natural easing. If you used Auto Keying, check for accidental keys and delete any you don't want. A typical refinement is to compress the timing between the first two bounces to suggest energy loss over time. This hands-on sequence builds the habit of planning poses, inserting keys intentionally, and using editors to refine timing and feel. After you finish, ask: does the bounce feel natural or mechanical, and which interpolation change improved it?

keyIdea.title: Practice
keyIdea.text: Use the bouncing ball exercise to block poses, insert keys, and refine timing with interpolation and the Dope Sheet.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Bouncing Ball: Step-by-Step
Timeline

Step-by-step activity

1. Start a new file. Add UV Sphere, rename to 'BouncingBall'. 2. Frame 1: move Z to 2 → press I → Location. 3. Frame 20: move Z to 0 → press I → Location. 4. Frame 40: move Z to 1.5 → press I → Location. 5. Frame 60: move Z to 0 → press I → Location. 6. Frame 80: move Z to 0.75 → press I → Location. 7. Play and observe.
Refinement steps
  • Open Dope Sheet, select Z-location keys, press T to change interpolation.
  • Use S to scale timing if bounces feel too slow or too fast.
  • Delete accidental keys from Auto Keying and re-block as needed.
Key Takeaway

Block first, then refine. Use the Dope Sheet to adjust rhythm after key poses are in place.

Check your understanding

Does changing to Bezier interpolation make the bounce feel more natural? Try it now and compare.

screens.title: Common Beginner Pitfalls & Fixes
screens.subtitle: Troubleshoot accidental keys, snapping, and robotic motion

narration.text: Beginners often run into a few recurring problems that slow learning. First, forgetting to set keyframes or accidentally moving the playhead means objects snap back to previous poses on playback. The fix is to confirm the playhead placement and insert a key deliberately when you want to record a pose. Second, leaving Auto Keying on during refinement records many small accidental keys. The remedy is to disable Auto Keying when polishing, and use manual insertion for intentional changes. Third, using only Linear interpolation makes motion appear robotic and unnatural; try Bezier to add ease-in and ease-out. Fourth, overwriting a key by inserting on the wrong frame will change earlier poses unexpectedly — use the Dope Sheet to review and restore timing by moving or deleting problematic keys. A practical troubleshooting routine: scrub the Timeline to locate unexpected motion, open the Dope Sheet to inspect keys, delete or move the offending keys, then replay. Iteration is the animator's friend; expect to refine timing repeatedly. After each fix, ask: is the motion reading correctly now, or do I need one more timing pass?

keyIdea.title: Troubleshooting
keyIdea.text: Common issues include accidental keys, wrong playhead placement, and overuse of linear interpolation; inspect with the Dope Sheet to fix them.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Common Beginner Pitfalls & Fixes
Common Mistakes

Troubleshoot typical errors

No key set — snapping occurs
Confirm the playhead and insert keys to lock poses in place.
Auto Key clutter
Toggle Auto Keying off during detailed edits and clean unwanted keys in the Dope Sheet.
Robotic motion from Linear
Use Bezier for more natural acceleration and deceleration.
Fix routine
  1. Scrub the Timeline to find the unexpected motion.
  2. Open the Dope Sheet to inspect keys across objects.
  3. Move, delete, or replace keys to restore intended timing.
  4. Play back and repeat until the motion reads correctly.
Key Takeaway

Use the Dope Sheet to find and fix accidental keys; iteration is normal when polishing motion.

Pro tip

Make a habit of playing back after every bulk edit to catch issues early.

narration.text: Let's summarize the most important terms you should remember after working through these lessons. First, Keyframe: it's the snapshot of an object's property at a specific frame and forms the backbone of your animation. Second, Timeline Editor: the horizontal editor where you place keys, scrub the playhead, and preview motion; it controls the overall timing of your scene. Third, Playhead: the vertical indicator that marks which frame is currently active for insertion and playback. Memorize how these three elements interact: the playhead sets the moment, the Timeline houses the keys, and keyframes store the values. A short practice: place a playhead at frame 10, set a key for location, then move it to frame 30 and set another — this reinforces the relationship. Keep these terms clear to avoid common mistakes like inserting keys at the wrong frame or misreading the Timeline. Which of these three will you test right now?

keyIdea.title: Core terms
keyIdea.text: Keyframe, Timeline, and Playhead are the foundational vocabulary for timing and pose placement.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Key Concepts — Part 1
Keyframe
A recorded value for a property at a specific frame.
Timeline Editor
Where keys live and where you control playback and frame ranges.
Playhead
The current frame marker used to insert or update keys.
Summary
Practice putting a playhead, inserting a key, and playing back to link these concepts with muscle memory.

narration.text: A few final concepts round out the chapter. Keyframe (the basic unit), Interpolation (how Blender fills in the frames), Dope Sheet Editor (for bulk timing edits), and Auto Keying (automatic insertion) form a practical vocabulary for everyday animation. Interpolation choices determine whether motion feels mechanical, abrupt, or natural; use Bezier for organic movement and Linear for constant motion. The Dope Sheet helps you move or scale many keys simultaneously so you can change rhythm quickly. Auto Keying speeds blocking but can create accidental keys, so toggle it off when refining. As a short exercise, animate two keys and switch interpolation to observe the change. Final takeaway: separate posing from timing — create clear key poses first, then use the Timeline and Dope Sheet to adjust rhythm, and finally refine interpolation for the right feel. Which editor will you open first to practice?

keyIdea.title: Editors & workflow
keyIdea.text: Use Timeline for placement, Dope Sheet for global timing, and interpolation choices to craft motion feeling; toggle Auto Keying with care.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Key Concepts — Part 2
Keyframe (again)
The recorded state for a property at a frame; the building block of animation.
Interpolation
Determines how frames between keys are calculated: Linear, Constant, Bezier, etc.
Dope Sheet
A timing workshop to move, scale, and edit groups of keys across objects.
Final summary
Separate posing from timing: block key poses, use editors to set rhythm, then refine interpolation for the right feel. Auto Keying is optional and best used for blocking only.
